<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1" />
<title>Iwasawa theory</title>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/katex@0.16.11/dist/katex.min.css">
<script defer src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/katex@0.16.11/dist/katex.min.js"></script>
<script defer src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/katex@0.16.11/dist/contrib/auto-render.min.js"></script>
<script>
(function(){
  function renderAll(){
    if(typeof renderMathInElement!=='function'){ return setTimeout(renderAll,50); }
    renderMathInElement(document.body,{
      delimiters:[
        {left:'$$',right:'$$',display:true},
        {left:'$',right:'$',display:false},
        {left:'\\(',right:'\\)',display:false},
        {left:'\\[',right:'\\]',display:true}
      ],
      throwOnError:false,
      macros:{
        '\\Spec':'\\operatorname{Spec}',
        '\\Gal':'\\operatorname{Gal}',
        '\\Hom':'\\operatorname{Hom}',
        '\\tr':'\\operatorname{tr}',
        '\\ad':'\\operatorname{ad}',
        '\\ind':'\\operatorname{ind}'
      }
    });
  }
  if(document.readyState==='loading') document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded',renderAll);
  else renderAll();
})();
</script>
<style>
  :root{
    --bg:#0f1218; --panel:#161b24; --panel2:#1c2230;
    --ink:#e8ecf1; --mute:#9aa4b2; --line:#2a3242;
    --yellow:#ffd866; --blue:#58c4dd; --green:#83c167;
    --pink:#e07a5f; --violet:#b39ddb; --cyan:#7de0d6;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  html,body{margin:0;padding:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
    font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Inter,Roboto,sans-serif;
    font-size:17px;line-height:1.65}
  a{color:var(--blue)}
  code{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;
    background:#0b0f16;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:4px;color:#f0c987;font-size:0.92em}
  main{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;padding:4rem 1.5rem 8rem}
  h1{font-size:2.4rem;letter-spacing:-0.01em;margin:0 0 0.4rem}
  h2{font-size:1.6rem;margin:3.2rem 0 0.8rem;color:#fff;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding-bottom:.4rem}
  h3{font-size:1.15rem;margin:1.8rem 0 .6rem;color:var(--yellow)}
  p{margin:0.7rem 0}
  .sub{color:var(--mute);margin-top:0;margin-bottom:2rem}
  .widget{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:10px;
    padding:1rem 1.1rem 1.2rem;margin:1.2rem 0}
  .widget .hd{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:baseline;margin-bottom:.6rem;gap:.8rem;flex-wrap:wrap}
  .widget .hd .ttl{font-weight:600;color:#fff;font-size:.95rem;letter-spacing:.02em;text-transform:uppercase}
  .widget .hd .hint{color:var(--mute);font-size:.85rem}
  .row{display:flex;gap:.6rem;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;margin:.4rem 0}
  .row label{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem}
  input[type="text"],input[type="number"],select{
    background:#0b0f16;color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .55rem;font-family:inherit;font-size:.95rem}
  input[type="range"]{accent-color:var(--yellow);flex:1;max-width:260px}
  button{background:var(--panel2);color:var(--ink);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:6px;padding:.35rem .7rem;cursor:pointer;font:inherit}
  button:hover{background:#242c3e}
  button.active{background:var(--yellow);color:#111;border-color:var(--yellow)}
  .readout{background:#0b0f16;border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:6px;
    padding:.6rem .8rem;font-family:ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:.92rem;color:#cbd5e1;
    min-height:1.6em;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word}
  .pill{display:inline-block;background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);
    border-radius:999px;padding:1px 8px;font-size:.82rem;color:var(--mute);margin-right:4px}
  .note{border-left:3px solid var(--violet);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d8d2ef;background:#1a1828;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .ok{border-left:3px solid var(--green);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#d5ebc8;background:#1a2418;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  .bad{border-left:3px solid var(--pink);padding:.3rem .9rem;color:#f4d2c7;background:#2a1a18;
    margin:1rem 0;border-radius:0 6px 6px 0}
  svg{display:block;margin:0 auto;max-width:100%}
  svg text{fill:var(--ink);font-family:inherit}
  nav.toc{position:sticky;top:0;background:rgba(15,18,24,.93);backdrop-filter:blur(8px);
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);padding:.6rem 1rem;z-index:10;
    display:flex;gap:1rem;flex-wrap:wrap;font-size:.9rem}
  nav.toc a{color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none}
  nav.toc a:hover{color:var(--yellow)}
  /* sticky sidebar TOC (wide screens only; narrow screens fall back to top-nav) */
  aside.sidetoc{position:fixed;top:4.2rem;
    left:max(1rem, calc(50% - 440px - 220px));
    width:200px;max-height:calc(100vh - 6rem);overflow-y:auto;
    padding-right:1rem;border-right:1px solid var(--line);
    font-size:.88rem;z-index:5}
  aside.sidetoc .sidetoc-title{font-size:.7rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute);margin:0 0 .5rem;padding-bottom:.35rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line)}
  aside.sidetoc ol{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc li{margin:0}
  aside.sidetoc a{display:block;padding:.3rem .5rem;color:var(--mute);text-decoration:none;
    border-left:2px solid transparent;line-height:1.35;
    transition:color 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease}
  aside.sidetoc a:hover{color:var(--ink)}
  aside.sidetoc a.active{color:var(--yellow);border-left-color:var(--yellow)}
  @media (max-width:1180px){ aside.sidetoc{display:none} }
  @media (min-width:1181px){ nav.toc a[href^="#"]{display:none} }
  .hero{padding:3rem 0 1rem}
  .small{font-size:.88rem;color:var(--mute)}
  footer{color:var(--mute);font-size:.88rem;text-align:center;margin-top:4rem}
  table.plain{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:.95rem;margin:.6rem 0}
  table.plain th,table.plain td{padding:.35rem .5rem;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);text-align:left}
  table.plain th{color:var(--mute);font-weight:500}
  /* callback-css-auto-begin */
  aside.callback{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:rgba(88,196,221,0.05);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--cyan) 45%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.callback .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.callback ul{margin:0;padding-left:1.1rem}
  aside.callback ul li{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.callback a{color:inherit}
/* callback-css-auto-end */
  details.changelog{
    margin:2rem 0 1rem;padding:.6rem .9rem;
    background:rgba(0,0,0,0.22);
    border-radius:6px;
    font-size:.85rem;
  }
  details.changelog summary{
    cursor:pointer;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;
    font-size:.7rem;color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);
  }
  details.changelog table{margin-top:.5rem;border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:.82rem}
  details.changelog td{padding:.2rem .6rem;border-bottom:1px dashed rgba(255,255,255,0.07);vertical-align:top}
  details.changelog td:first-child{color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);white-space:nowrap;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  aside.related{
    margin:1.2rem 0;padding:.7rem 1rem;
    background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 6%, transparent);
    border-left:3px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--mute) 55%, transparent);
    border-radius:0 6px 6px 0;
    font-size:.93rem;
  }
  aside.related .ttl{
    font-size:.68rem;letter-spacing:.14em;text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--mute,#8c9aa6);margin-bottom:.3rem;font-weight:600;
  }
  aside.related > div{margin:.15rem 0}
  aside.related .more{color:var(--mute);font-style:italic}
  aside.related a{color:inherit}
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-begin */
  html[data-hide-widgets] .widget { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-quizzes] .quiz { display: none !important; }
  html[data-hide-lineage] .lineage-strip { display: none !important; }
  .mv-display-toggles { display: inline-flex; gap: .6rem; align-items: center; }
  .mv-display-toggle { background: transparent; border: 1px solid var(--line, #333); border-radius: 6px; padding: 5px 10px; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1.05rem; line-height: 1; color: inherit; transition: background 120ms ease, border-color 120ms ease; }
  .mv-display-toggle:hover { background: var(--panel, rgba(255,255,255,0.06)); border-color: var(--mute, #666); }
  .mv-display-toggle--off { opacity: 0.35; }
  /* display-prefs-css-auto-end */
</style>

Iwasawa theory

Climb the cyclotomic tower and watch class groups, Selmer groups, and special $L$-values fall into the structure of a single power-series ring. From Iwasawa's $\mu,\lambda,\nu$ invariants to the Mazur–Wiles main conjecture and its elliptic descendant.

blocks.html:
1. The cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension

Iwasawa's idea is to study a number field $K$ not in isolation but along a tower $$K = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset K_2 \subset \cdots \subset K_\infty = \bigcup_n K_n,$$ where each $K_n/K$ is Galois with $\Gal(K_n/K)\cong\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ and so $\Gamma=\Gal(K_\infty/K)\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$. The plan is to read off finite-level invariants from a single object attached to the whole tower.

Over $K=\mathbb{Q}$ there is a canonical such tower, the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension. Adjoin all $p$-power roots of unity: $$\Gal(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{p^\infty})/\mathbb{Q})\;\cong\;\mathbb{Z}_p^\times.$$ For odd $p$ this group splits as $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times\times(1+p\mathbb{Z}_p)\cong\mathbb{Z}/(p-1)\times\mathbb{Z}_p$. The unique $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension $\mathbb{Q}_\infty/\mathbb{Q}$ is the fixed field of the torsion part $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$. Concretely: for $p=2$ it is the cyclotomic-real tower $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{2^\infty})^+$; for odd $p$ it is the unique $\mathbb{Z}_p$-quotient of the full cyclotomic tower.

Iwasawa's growth formula. Let $A_n$ be the $p$-part of the ideal class group of $K_n$. Iwasawa proved there exist non-negative integers $\mu, \lambda$ and an integer $\nu$ such that $$|A_n|\;=\;p^{\,\mu p^n + \lambda n + \nu}\qquad\text{for all }n\gg 0.$$ The slogan: $p$-class numbers grow at a rate dictated by an exponential ($\mu$), a linear ($\lambda$), and a constant ($\nu$) term — and the three numbers are invariants of the tower.

The widget below evaluates the formula. Move the sliders for $\mu, \lambda, \nu$ and watch $\log_p|A_n|$ track the growth. Set $\mu=0$ and you see the linear-only regime guaranteed for cyclotomic towers over abelian fields by Ferrero–Washington (proved in §3).

<script>
/* =========== SECTION 1: Iwasawa growth formula widget =========== */
(function(){
  const svg=$('#g-svg'), out=$('#g-out');
  const muS=$('#g-mu'), lamS=$('#g-lam'), nuS=$('#g-nu'), pS=$('#g-p');
  const muV=$('#g-mu-val'), lamV=$('#g-lam-val'), nuV=$('#g-nu-val');

  function exp(n,mu,lam,nu,p){ return mu*Math.pow(p,n)+lam*n+nu; }

  function render(){
    const mu=+muS.value, lam=+lamS.value, nu=+nuS.value, p=+pS.value;
    muV.textContent=mu; lamV.textContent=lam; nuV.textContent=nu;
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    const W=620,H=280, padL=60,padR=24,padT=24,padB=44;
    const Nmax=8;
    let yMax=1;
    for(let n=0;n<=Nmax;n++) yMax=Math.max(yMax,Math.abs(exp(n,mu,lam,nu,p)));
    yMax=Math.max(yMax, 1);
    const x = n => padL + (W-padL-padR)*n/Nmax;
    const y = v => padT + (H-padT-padB)*(1 - v/yMax);
    // axes
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:padL,y1:H-padB,x2:W-padR,y2:H-padB,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':1}));
    svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:padL,y1:padT,x2:padL,y2:H-padB,stroke:'var(--mute)','stroke-width':1}));
    // axis labels + ticks
    for(let n=0;n<=Nmax;n++){
      svg.appendChild(SVG('line',{x1:x(n),y1:H-padB,x2:x(n),y2:H-padB+4,stroke:'var(--mute)'}));
      const t=SVG('text',{x:x(n),y:H-padB+18,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':11,fill:'var(--mute)'});
      t.textContent=n; svg.appendChild(t);
    }
    const xl=SVG('text',{x:(W+padL-padR)/2,y:H-8,'text-anchor':'middle','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    xl.textContent='layer index n'; svg.appendChild(xl);
    const yl=SVG('text',{x:padL-44,y:padT+12,'text-anchor':'start','font-size':12,fill:'var(--mute)'});
    yl.textContent='log_p |A_n|'; svg.appendChild(yl);
    // points + line
    let path='';
    const pts=[];
    for(let n=0;n<=Nmax;n++){
      const v=exp(n,mu,lam,nu,p);
      const cx=x(n), cy=y(v);
      pts.push([n,v,cx,cy]);
      path += (n===0?'M':' L') + cx + ' ' + cy;
    }
    svg.appendChild(SVG('path',{d:path,fill:'none',stroke:'var(--yellow)','stroke-width':2}));
    for(const [n,v,cx,cy] of pts){
      svg.appendChild(SVG('circle',{cx,cy,r:4,fill:'var(--yellow)'}));
    }
    // readout
    const lines=[];
    for(let n=0;n<=4;n++){
      const v=exp(n,mu,lam,nu,p);
      const sz=v>=0 && v<=20 ? `|A_${n}|=${p}^${v}=${Math.pow(p,v)}` : `log_${p}|A_${n}|=${v}`;
      lines.push(sz);
    }
    out.textContent = `formula: log_${p}|A_n| = ${mu}·${p}^n + ${lam}·n + ${nu}\n` + lines.join('   ');
  }
  [muS,lamS,nuS,pS].forEach(s=>s.addEventListener('input',render));
  render();
})();
</script>

blocks.html:
For a general number field $K$, the number of independent $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions of $K$ is $r_2(K)+1+\delta$ where $\delta\ge 0$ is the Leopoldt defect. Leopoldt's conjecture (still open in general) says $\delta=0$, so $K$ has exactly $r_2(K)+1$ independent towers — and the cyclotomic one is one of them.

2. The Iwasawa algebra $\Lambda$

Fix $\Gamma\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$ with topological generator $\gamma$. The natural ring acting on objects attached to the tower is the completed group algebra $$\Lambda \;=\; \mathbb{Z}_p[[\Gamma]] \;=\; \varprojlim_n\;\mathbb{Z}_p[\Gamma/\Gamma^{p^n}].$$ The crucial computation, due to Serre, is that $\Lambda$ is no mystery — it is a power-series ring in disguise.

Serre's identification. The map $\gamma\mapsto 1+T$ extends to a topological isomorphism $$\mathbb{Z}_p[[\Gamma]] \;\xrightarrow{\,\sim\,}\; \mathbb{Z}_p[[T]],\qquad T = \gamma-1.$$ So $\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_p[[T]]$: a complete, regular, local Noetherian ring of Krull dimension 2 with maximal ideal $(p,T)$.

The non-zero elements split into a distinguished form via the Weierstrass preparation theorem: every $f\in\Lambda$ with $f\ne 0$ can be written uniquely as $f = p^\mu \cdot u(T)\cdot P(T)$ with $u\in\Lambda^\times$ a unit and $P(T)=T^\lambda + a_{\lambda-1}T^{\lambda-1}+\cdots+a_0$ a distinguished polynomial ($p\mid a_i$ for $i<\lambda$). The numbers $\mu,\lambda$ here are the same letters that appear in Iwasawa's growth formula — by design.

Structure theorem (Serre, after Iwasawa). Every finitely generated $\Lambda$-module $M$ admits a $\Lambda$-homomorphism to a "standard" module $$E(M) \;=\; \Lambda^r \;\oplus\; \bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}\Lambda/(p^{a_i}) \;\oplus\; \bigoplus_{j=1}^{t}\Lambda/(f_j(T)^{m_j}),$$ with $f_j$ distinguished irreducible, whose kernel and cokernel are both finite (a pseudo-isomorphism $M\sim E(M)$). The data $(r;a_i;f_j,m_j)$ is unique.

Two invariants fall out of $E(M)$:

  • the $\Lambda$-rank $\operatorname{rank}_\Lambda M = r$;
  • the characteristic ideal $\operatorname{char}_\Lambda M = \Big(p^{\sum a_i}\,\prod_j f_j(T)^{m_j}\Big)\subset\Lambda$, defined when $r=0$ (i.e. $M$ is $\Lambda$-torsion).

The widget builds an example $\Lambda$-module summand and reads off its characteristic ideal and the corresponding $(\mu, \lambda)$ contribution. The $\mu$-piece contributes $a$ to $\mu$; the polynomial piece contributes $\deg f \cdot m$ to $\lambda$.

    }

  }

3. Class groups along the tower

Now turn $\Lambda$ on a real arithmetic object. For each $n$ let $A_n=\operatorname{Cl}(K_n)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$, the $p$-Sylow of the ideal class group of the $n$-th layer. The norm maps $A_{n+1}\to A_n$ assemble into an inverse limit $$X_\infty \;=\; \varprojlim_n A_n,$$ and the action of $\Gamma$ on each $K_n$ extends by continuity to a $\Lambda$-module action on $X_\infty$.

Iwasawa (1959). $X_\infty$ is finitely generated as a $\Lambda$-module. That $X_\infty$ is also $\Lambda$-torsion is conjectural in general; it follows for abelian $K/\mathbb{Q}$ from Ferrero–Washington (1979) plus Iwasawa's class-number bounds, and was proved for totally real $K$ by Wiles (1990) as part of the totally-real main conjecture. Granting torsion, $X_\infty$ has well-defined invariants $$\mu(K_\infty/K),\;\lambda(K_\infty/K),\;\operatorname{char}_\Lambda(X_\infty)\subset\Lambda,$$ and the growth formula $$|A_n|\;=\;p^{\,\mu p^n+\lambda n+\nu}\qquad(n\gg 0)$$ follows by counting $\Gamma$-coinvariants level by level.

The proof reads norm growth off the structure theorem. Each $\Lambda/(p^a)$ summand contributes $a\cdot p^n$ to $\log_p|A_n|$ (because $|\Lambda/(p^a, T^{p^n}-1)| = p^{a p^n}$); each $\Lambda/(f^m)$ summand with $f$ distinguished of degree $d$ contributes $dm\cdot n$ (eventually). The constant $\nu$ collects bounded boundary terms.

Ferrero–Washington (1979). For the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of any abelian number field, $\mu = 0$.

So the exponential rate vanishes and class numbers grow only linearly in $n$. The same statement for non-abelian base fields, or for non-cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions of non-CM fields, is open. The widget below tabulates the predicted sizes $|A_n|$ from invariants $(\mu,\lambda,\nu)$ and lets you compare two candidate towers side by side — pre-Ferrero–Washington one might worry that $\mu>0$, the curve on the right shows what that would mean.

blocks.html:
An elegant consequence: the $\Gamma$-coinvariants $X_\infty/(T-(\gamma-1))X_\infty$ recover $A_0=A=\operatorname{Cl}(K)_p$. Specialising the characteristic ideal at $T=0$ therefore reads off (a multiple of) the class number. This is the first hint of the main conjecture: a single power-series-valued invariant of the tower secretly encodes every level's class number.

4. $p$-adic $L$-functions

The other half of the main conjecture is analytic: a function on $\mathbb{Z}_p$ that interpolates classical Dirichlet $L$-values $p$-adically.

Kubota–Leopoldt (1964). For each non-trivial Dirichlet character $\chi$ of conductor coprime to $p$ there is a unique continuous function $L_p(\,\cdot\,,\chi)\colon\mathbb{Z}_p\to\mathbb{C}_p$ such that for every integer $n\ge 1$: $$L_p(1-n,\chi) \;=\; \big(1-\chi\omega^{-n}(p)\,p^{n-1}\big)\,L(1-n,\chi\omega^{-n}).$$ Here $\omega\colon(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times\to\mathbb{Z}_p^\times$ is the Teichmüller character (the unique character lifting the identity on residues).

The right-hand side is a classical Dirichlet $L$-value, with the Euler factor at $p$ stripped out. The non-trivial content is that these infinitely many values, evaluated at unrelated integers, fit together into a single $p$-adically continuous (in fact, analytic on each residue disk) function on $\mathbb{Z}_p$. The mechanism is

Kummer congruences. Classical fact: if $n\equiv m\pmod{(p-1)p^{k-1}}$ and $(p-1)\nmid n$, then for the Riemann zeta function $$\frac{(1-p^{n-1})\,\zeta(1-n)}{n}\;\equiv\;\frac{(1-p^{m-1})\,\zeta(1-m)}{m}\pmod{p^k}.$$ Equivalently $B_n/n\equiv B_m/m\pmod{p^k}$ in this regime — the values that $L_p$ interpolates are $p$-adically continuous in $n$. Kummer noticed this for the class numbers of cyclotomic fields; Kubota–Leopoldt promoted it to a genuine analytic function.

The widget below verifies a Kummer congruence numerically. Pick $p$ and a target precision $k$; the table prints $\zeta(1-n)\cdot(1-p^{n-1})$ at $n$'s lying in a fixed residue class mod $(p-1)p^{k-1}$ and shows how many $p$-adic digits agree.

blocks.html:
A second packaging is closer to the main-conjecture statement. Via Mahler's theorem there is a power series $L_p(\chi,T)\in\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}_p$, the Iwasawa power series attached to $\chi$, such that $$L_p(s,\chi)\;=\;L_p(\chi,\,\langle\kappa\rangle^{s}-1)$$ for $\kappa$ a topological generator of $1+p\mathbb{Z}_p$. So $L_p$ is, structurally, an element of the same Iwasawa algebra $\Lambda$ that controls $X_\infty$. That coincidence of habitat is the entire point.

5. The Iwasawa main conjecture

Two objects, both finitely-generated torsion $\Lambda$-modules, both attached to the cyclotomic tower:

algebraic sideanalytic side
object$X_\infty=\varprojlim A_n$$L_p(\chi,T)\in\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}_p$
invariant$\operatorname{char}_\Lambda(X_\infty)$ideal $(L_p(\chi,T))$
built fromclass groupsBernoulli numbers $/$ $L$-values
Iwasawa main conjecture. Decompose $X_\infty$ under the prime-to-$p$ Galois action of $\Gal(\mathbb{Q}(\mu_p)/\mathbb{Q})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$ into character eigenspaces. Then for each odd character $\chi$, $$\operatorname{char}_\Lambda\!\big(X_\infty(\chi)\big) \;=\; \big(L_p(\chi^{-1}\omega,T)\big) \quad\text{in }\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}_p.$$ Equivalently: the algebraically-defined characteristic ideal equals the analytically-defined $p$-adic $L$-ideal.
Mazur–Wiles (1984). The conjecture holds for abelian extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$.
Wiles (1990). The analogous statement holds for any totally real number field $K$.

The strategy in both proofs threads through modular forms: cusp forms whose Galois representations have residual reducibility let one congruence Eisenstein series (whose constant term is a Dirichlet $L$-value) with cusp forms (whose Galois reps cut out unramified extensions, hence class groups). Specialising the congruence at any $\Gamma$-character extracts the equality of $L$-ideals. The same two-step (Eisenstein congruences $+$ Galois deformation) reappears in §6 for elliptic curves.

Specialisations recover classics. Send $T\to 0$ in $\operatorname{char}_\Lambda(X_\infty(\chi))=(L_p(\chi^{-1}\omega,T))$ to get the analytic class number formula in the form $$\#A_0(\chi) \;\doteq\; L_p(0,\chi^{-1}\omega) \;\doteq\; -\tfrac{1}{n}\,B_{n,\chi^{-1}\omega}\;\;\text{at the appropriate twist},$$ recovering Herbrand's theorem (an irregular prime $p$ divides $B_k$ implies a non-trivial $\omega^{1-k}$-eigenspace in the class group of $\mathbb{Q}(\mu_p)$) — and Ribet's converse, which is one of the building blocks of the proof.

The widget below compares the two ideals on a single concrete factor. Pick a distinguished polynomial $f(T)$ — pretend it was found two ways: as the characteristic generator on the algebraic side, and as the Iwasawa power series on the analytic side. The conjecture says these agree up to a unit.

    const f=fS.value, u=uS.value;
    const lhs = `algebraic:  char_Λ(X_∞(χ)) = ${FLAB[f]}`;
    const rhs = `analytic:   (L_p(χ^{-1}ω, T))    = (${u})·${FLAB[f]}  =  ${FLAB[f]}  (since unit ${u} ∈ Λ^×)`;
    const eq  = `equal as ideals in Λ ⊗ ℚ_p  ✓  (Mazur–Wiles for abelian /ℚ; Wiles for totally real)`;
    out.textContent = lhs + '\n' + rhs + '\n\n' + eq;
  }
  [fS,uS].forEach(s=>s.addEventListener('change',render));
  render();
})();
</script>

6. Elliptic Iwasawa theory and BSD

Iwasawa's tower-of-class-groups picture was extended by Mazur (1972) to elliptic curves. Replace the $p$-class group $A_n$ with the $p^\infty$-Selmer group along the cyclotomic tower: $$\mathrm{Sel}_{p^\infty}(E/K_n) \;=\; \ker\Big(H^1(K_n, E[p^\infty])\to\prod_v H^1(K_{n,v},E)\Big).$$ The Mordell–Weil group $E(K_n)\otimes\mathbb{Q}_p/\mathbb{Z}_p$ injects into the Selmer group; the cokernel is the $p^\infty$-Tate–Shafarevich group. Take limits: $$X_E \;=\; \big(\varinjlim_n\,\mathrm{Sel}_{p^\infty}(E/K_n)\big)^\vee.$$ This Pontryagin dual carries a $\Lambda$-action.

Mazur's control theorem (1972). If $E$ has good ordinary reduction at $p$, then $X_E$ is a finitely generated $\Lambda$-module, and $\Gamma$-coinvariants recover $\mathrm{Sel}_{p^\infty}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ up to a finite controlled error.
Elliptic main conjecture (Mazur–Swinnerton-Dyer; Greenberg). Conjecturally $X_E$ is $\Lambda$-torsion and $$\operatorname{char}_\Lambda(X_E)\;=\;\big(L_p(E,T)\big)\quad\text{in }\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{Q}_p,$$ where $L_p(E,T)$ is the Mazur–Swinnerton-Dyer $p$-adic $L$-function attached to $E$, interpolating the classical $L$-values $L(E,\chi,1)/(\Omega_E\cdot\text{periods})$ along characters $\chi$ of $\Gamma$.

Three landmark results give it teeth:

  • Coates–Wiles (1977) + later refinements: if $E$ has CM by $\mathcal{O}_K$ with $K$ imaginary quadratic of class number $1$ and $L(E,1)\ne 0$, then $E(\mathbb{Q})$ is finite (Coates–Wiles, Inventiones 1977). The class-number-1 hypothesis was later removed by Arthaud, Coates–Goldstein, and Rubin. This was the first weak BSD result for any infinite family of curves, and the prototype for using a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension to prove a global rank bound.
  • Kato (2000s): an Euler system in the $K$-theory of modular curves provides the divisibility $\operatorname{char}_\Lambda(X_E)\,\Big|\,(L_p(E,T))$ for any modular elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$.
  • Skinner–Urban (2014): the converse divisibility via Eisenstein congruences on $\mathrm{GU}(2,2)$, completing the equality of ideals (under technical hypotheses) for many ordinary curves.
Consequence: $p$-part of BSD. Combined, these give the $p$-part of the BSD formula $$L^{(r)}(E,1)/r! \;\doteq\; \frac{\#\Sha(E/\mathbb{Q})\cdot\operatorname{Reg}\cdot\prod c_v}{(\#E(\mathbb{Q})_{\text{tors}})^2}$$ for many $E/\mathbb{Q}$ of analytic rank $r\le 1$ — including the finiteness of $\Sha$ at the prime $p$.

The widget pairs a curve with its $p$-adic $L$-function and reads off whether each ingredient — Coates–Wiles (CM), Kato divisibility, Skinner–Urban divisibility, and main-conjecture equality — applies. Toggle the curve type and reduction to see how much of the dictionary is unconditionally proved today.

<script>
/* =========== SECTION 6: who's-proved-what widget =========== */
(function(){
  const cm=$('#el-cm'), red=$('#el-red'), ar=$('#el-ar'), out=$('#el-out');
  function render(){
    const isCM = cm.value==='cm';
    const r = red.value;
    const a = +ar.value;
    const lines=[];
    // Coates-Wiles
    if(isCM && a===0){
      lines.push('  ✓ Coates–Wiles (1977): L(E,1) ≠ 0 + CM ⇒ rank 0 (E(ℚ) finite).');
    } else if(isCM){
      lines.push('  – Coates–Wiles applies only when a-rank = 0; here a-rank > 0.');
    } else {
      lines.push('  – Coates–Wiles requires CM; this curve is non-CM.');
    }
    // Kato divisibility (modular elliptic curves over Q)
    if(r==='ord'){
      lines.push('  ✓ Kato (Euler system): char_Λ(X_E) | (L_p(E,T)) — modularity supplies the input.');
    } else if(r==='mult'){
      lines.push('  ✓ Kato also covers multiplicative reduction.');
    } else {
      lines.push('  ▲ Kato in the supersingular case requires Pollack/Sprung ± L_p; signed main conjectures.');
    }
    // Skinner-Urban
    if(r==='ord' && !isCM){
      lines.push('  ✓ Skinner–Urban (2014): (L_p(E,T)) | char_Λ(X_E) under standard hypotheses.');
    } else if(r==='ord' && isCM){
      lines.push('  ✓ Rubin (CM case, 1991) provides the converse divisibility.');
    } else {
      lines.push('  ▲ Converse divisibility in supersingular/multiplicative cases is still partial.');
    }
    // p-part of BSD
    if(a<=1 && r==='ord'){
      lines.push('  ⇒ p-part of BSD known (mod hypotheses) for analytic rank ≤ 1.');
    } else if(a>=2){
      lines.push('  ▲ Analytic rank ≥ 2 is wide open: even nonvanishing of leading L-coefficient is conjectural.');
    }
    out.textContent = `curve: ${isCM?'CM':'non-CM'},  reduction: ${r},  analytic rank: ${a}\n\n` + lines.join('\n');
  }
  [cm,red,ar].forEach(s=>s.addEventListener('change',render));
  render();
})();
</script>

Connections

Iwasawa's tower-and-power-series machine has migrated far beyond its 1959 origin. The two open frontiers a beginner is most likely to meet are Greenberg's conjecture ($\lambda=0$ for the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of a totally real field — still open even for $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$) and the full elliptic main conjecture at supersingular primes (the Selmer group is no longer $\Lambda$-torsion; one needs Pollack–Sprung's signed $\pm$-Selmer groups and matching $\pm$-$L$-functions). On the modern side, Iwasawa-theoretic Euler systems and deformation-theoretic Eisenstein congruences feed directly into the Bloch–Kato conjecture and the proof of Sato–Tate for Hilbert modular forms.

  • Class field theory — Hilbert class field — the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension is built inside the abelianized Galois group whose existence is class-field-theoretic.
  • $p$-adic numbers — Iwasawa's whole world (the algebra $\Lambda$, the $L$-functions, the topology of class group limits) lives over $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
  • $L$-functions — special values — the values $L(1-n,\chi)$ that $L_p$ interpolates are exactly the special values that BSD-style refined formulas predict.
  • Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer — elliptic Iwasawa theory gives the strongest unconditional $p$-part-of-BSD results known.
  • Galois representations — modularity and deformations — Skinner–Urban and Wiles run on the same Eisenstein-congruence engine that powers $R=T$ theorems.
  • Modularity and FLT — Iwasawa-theoretic deformation rings supply the input to modularity, which in turn feeds Kato's Euler system.
